mainTopic: Windows and מחיצות, then neighbors' damages: mills, ovens, storerooms and noise in a courtyard
overview: The גמרא finishes a ברייתא about items placed in a window. Such an item makes the opening smaller only if the owner will leave it there, so a shard, a כלי חרס and a ספר תורה each count only when they are useless or set aside for good. Because salt is mentioned, the גמרא brings רב and שמואל on building a מחיצה from salt. It settles their dispute two ways: by the type of salt, or by whether a beam presses the salt down. Next it explains the משנה's distances: a mill is kept from the wall because of its noise, not its shaking, and אביי learns the shape of an oven from its measurements. A new משנה sets rules for ovens near ceilings and floors. The תנא קמא and רבי שמעון disagree on whether keeping the distances frees you from paying for damage. It also forbids putting a bakery, dye shop or cattle barn under a neighbor's storeroom, with an exception for wine. The גמרא discusses all of these, leaving several questions as תיקו. Finally, a משנה about noise in a shared courtyard begins, and אביי and רבא start explaining why a store may be blocked but noisy crafts may not. רבא's answer continues on the next amud.

steps.title: The shard is too small to matter
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers why a shard (חרס) shrinks the window: it is smaller than the size that counts as a real object.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is a case where the shard does not have the minimum size.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is answering a question from just before this text: why would a shard count as staying in the window? It says the shard is too small to be considered a real item.
steps.deeperAnalysis: An item only shrinks the window if the owner will leave it there. A shard below the minimum שיעור is worthless, so nobody will bother taking it back. That makes it a permanent part of the window.

keyTerms.meaning: the minimum size or measure for something to count
a piece of broken earthenware, a shard
shrinks or reduces the size of an opening

phrases.english: Where it does not have the minimum measure;

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge about חרס that comes just before this text.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Narrowing the case: the shard is below the minimum size
steps.terutzHavaAmina: A shard is useful, so the owner would take it back.
steps.terutzMaskana: A shard this small is worthless, so it stays in the window and shrinks it.

steps.title: Source for the minimum size of a shard
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא cites a משנה in שבת that defines how big a shard must be to count.
steps.simpleTranslation: As we learned in a משנה: a shard counts if it is big enough to place between one board and another.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes a משנה to show where the minimum size of a shard comes from.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה in שבת says carrying a shard is only significant if it is big enough to wedge between stacked boards or pillars. Anything smaller is not worth anything. Our shard is smaller than that, so it is treated as nothing.

keyTerms.meaning: as we learned in a משנה
boards or pillars piled on the ground
to its fellow, the next one

phrases.english: As we learned in a Mishnah: a shard –
enough to place between one board and another.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports step 1 by giving the source for the minimum size.
steps.raayaObject: The minimum שיעור for a shard to count as significant
steps.raayaSupportSource: The משנה in שבת about carrying a shard on שבת

steps.title: But an earthenware vessel is useful
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא says a כלי חרס shrinks the window. The גמרא objects that it is still usable.
steps.simpleTranslation: An earthenware vessel? But it is fit for him to use!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves to the next item in the ברייתא and challenges it. A usable vessel will probably be taken back, so how can it count as staying in the window?
steps.deeperAnalysis: The same rule applies: only an item the owner will leave behind shrinks the window. A whole earthenware vessel has obvious uses, so it seems temporary.

keyTerms.meaning: it is fit for him (to use)

phrases.english: An earthenware vessel – it is fit for him!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves on from the shard to the next item listed in the ברייתא.
steps.kashyaTarget: The ברייתא's ruling that a כלי חרס shrinks the window
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A usable vessel will be taken back, so it should not count as a permanent part of the window.

steps.title: The vessel is dirty
steps.stepSummary: The vessel is too dirty for anyone to want it.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is a case where it is dirty.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the ברייתא is talking about a dirty vessel, which nobody wants to use.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A filthy vessel is useless for normal purposes. So the owner gives up on it and leaves it in the window.

phrases.english: Where it is dirty.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 3.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The vessel is usable, so it will be taken back.
steps.terutzMaskana: A dirty vessel is unwanted and stays in the window.

steps.title: But a bloodletter can still use it
steps.stepSummary: Even a dirty vessel is useful to a bloodletter.
steps.simpleTranslation: But it is fit for a bloodletter!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back: a bloodletter does not care if the vessel is dirty, so it is still useful.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A bloodletter only needs something to catch blood, and dirt makes no difference to him. So being dirty does not make the vessel worthless.

keyTerms.meaning: a bloodletter, someone who lets blood for healing

phrases.english: It is fit for a bloodletter!
phrases.notes: Here אומנא means a bloodletter, who could use even a dirty vessel to catch the blood.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the answer of step 4.
steps.kashyaTarget: The answer that a dirty vessel is useless
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A bloodletter would still use a dirty vessel, so it still has value.

steps.title: The vessel has a hole
steps.stepSummary: The vessel has a hole, so it cannot even hold blood.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is a case where it has a hole.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the vessel has a hole in it, so even a bloodletter cannot use it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A vessel with a hole cannot hold liquid at all. Now it is truly useless, so the owner leaves it in the window.

keyTerms.meaning: that it has a hole, is perforated

steps.whatToRemember: An item shrinks the window only when it is useless enough that the owner will leave it there. The גמרא keeps narrowing the case until that is true.

phrases.english: Where it is perforated.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 5.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: A bloodletter would take it back.
steps.terutzMaskana: A vessel with a hole cannot hold blood, so it stays.

steps.title: But a ספר תורה is for reading
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא says a ספר תורה shrinks the window. The גמרא objects that it is meant to be read.
steps.simpleTranslation: A ספר תורה? But it is fit for reading!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves to another item in the ברייתא. A ספר תורה will surely be taken back to read from, so how can it count as staying in the window?
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is the same question as before, now about a holy object. Something people read from regularly is clearly not left in a window for good.

phrases.english: A Torah scroll – it is fit for reading!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves on to the next item listed in the ברייתא.
steps.kashyaTarget: The ברייתא's ruling that a ספר תורה shrinks the window
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A usable ספר תורה will be taken back for reading.

steps.title: The scroll is worn out
steps.stepSummary: The scroll is too worn out to read from.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is a worn-out one.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the ברייתא means a worn-out ספר תורה that can no longer be read.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Once the scroll is too worn to read, it no longer has its normal use. That seems to make it something the owner would leave in place.

phrases.english: With a worn-out one.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 7.
steps.terutzMaskana: It is a worn-out scroll that cannot be read.

steps.title: But a worn-out scroll needs burial
steps.stepSummary: A worn-out ספר תורה must be put in a גניזה, so it will be moved anyway.
steps.simpleTranslation: But it needs to be stored away in a גניזה!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges again. Even a worn-out ספר תורה must be put away in a גניזה, so the owner will still take it from the window.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A worn-out scroll cannot simply be left anywhere. It has to be put away respectfully, and that requirement would make him move it.

keyTerms.meaning: respectful storage or burial for worn-out holy books

phrases.english: But it requires storing away!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the answer of step 8.
steps.kashyaTarget: The answer that a worn-out scroll stays in the window
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The requirement of גניזה means it will be removed and put away.

steps.title: The window itself is its גניזה
steps.stepSummary: The owner decided to make the window the scroll's place of גניזה.
steps.simpleTranslation: Its גניזה will be there.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the owner chose the window itself as the scroll's resting place, so it will never be moved.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The גניזה requirement does not force him to move it, because the window becomes the גניזה. Since he plans to leave it there for good, it shrinks the window.
steps.whatToRemember: For every item in the ברייתא, the key question is whether the owner will leave it there. Even a ספר תורה counts if he chose the window as its permanent גניזה.

phrases.english: There will be its storing away.
phrases.notes: He means the owner decided the window itself will be the scroll's final resting place.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 9.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Redefining the case by the owner's intention
steps.terutzHavaAmina: He will take it away for גניזה.
steps.terutzMaskana: The window is its גניזה, so it stays permanently.

steps.title: רב: any material works for a מחיצה except salt and fat
steps.stepSummary: רב rules that a מחיצה may be made of anything except salt and fat.
steps.simpleTranslation: And רב said: A barrier may be made from anything except salt and fat.
steps.whatsHappening: Because the ברייתא mentions salt, the גמרא brings a related ruling of רב about building a מחיצה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A מחיצה has to last. Salt crumbles and fat melts, so רב says they cannot be used. This ties back to the ברייתא's question of whether salt counts in a window.

phrases.english: And Rav said:
With anything one may make a barrier,
except for salt and fat.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new topic connected to the salt mentioned in the ברייתא.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Any material may serve as a מחיצה except salt and fat.

steps.title: שמואל: even salt works
steps.stepSummary: שמואל disagrees and allows a מחיצה made of salt.
steps.simpleTranslation: And שמואל said: Even salt.
steps.whatsHappening: שמואל gives the opposite ruling: salt may also be used for a מחיצה. This sets up an apparent argument for the גמרא to resolve next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב excluded salt, and שמואל includes it. It looks like a direct disagreement about whether salt is solid enough.

phrases.english: And Shmuel said: Even salt.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Disagrees with רב's exclusion of salt.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Salt may be used for a מחיצה.

steps.title: רב פפא: two different kinds of salt
steps.stepSummary: רב פפא explains that רב and שמואל do not really disagree. They are talking about different kinds of salt.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב פפא said: They do not disagree. This one is about Sodomite salt, and that one is about איסתרוקנית salt.
steps.whatsHappening: רב פפא resolves the apparent argument. שמואל allows hard salt from סדום, and רב forbids loose, grainy sea salt.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Sodomite salt is hard like stone, so it lasts and can be a wall. איסתרוקנית salt is made of loose grains that fall apart, so it cannot. Each אמורא was speaking about a different kind of salt.

keyTerms.meaning: salt from סדום, hard like stone

steps.whatToRemember: Salt can serve as a מחיצה only if it is the hard, stone-like Sodomite kind. Loose, grainy salt cannot.
steps.confusionAlert: Do not mix up which הא goes with which opinion. The first הא, Sodomite salt, matches שמואל, who allows salt. The second הא, the crumbly salt, matches רב, who does not.

phrases.english: Rav Pappa said: And they do not disagree –
this one is with Sodomite salt,
phrases.notes: This is שמואל's case. Hard salt that stands like stone.

phrases.english: that one is with Isterokanit salt.
phrases.notes: This is רב's case. Grainy salt that crumbles apart.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Settles the apparent dispute between steps 11 and 12.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Splitting the cases: each opinion speaks about a different kind of salt
steps.terutzHavaAmina: רב and שמואל argue about all salt.
steps.terutzMaskana: Hard Sodomite salt works for a מחיצה. Grainy salt does not.

steps.title: A second way to settle רב and שמואל: salt with a beam on top
steps.stepSummary: Based on רבה's ruling that a beam can rest on two piles of salt, even the weaker kind of salt can work. So רב, who forbids salt, means salt with no beam, and שמואל, who allows salt, means salt with a beam.
steps.simpleTranslation: Now that רבה said a person may make two piles of salt and put a beam on them, because the salt holds up the beam and the beam holds the salt in place, even the weaker איסתרוקנית salt works. So רב and שמואל do not disagree: one is talking about salt with a beam, and the other about salt with no beam.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא offers a new answer to the question of how רב and שמואל can disagree about salt. It uses רבה's ruling to say they are talking about different cases: with a beam and without a beam.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב פפא said the difference was the type of salt. רבה's ruling shows that a beam pressing down holds even weak salt together. So the real difference is whether there is a beam: שמואל, who allows salt, is talking about salt with a beam, and רב, who forbids it, is talking about salt with no beam.

keyTerms.meaning: A beam laid across the entrance of an alley
A softer kind of salt that falls apart more easily
This one is talking about... that one is talking about... (a way of splitting two rulings into two cases)

steps.whatToRemember: With a beam on top, salt holds together and can serve as a barrier (שמואל). Without a beam, it cannot (רב).

phrases.english: And now that Rabba said:
A person may make two piles of salt
and place a beam on top of them,
phrases.notes: This is the beam laid across an alley's entrance so people may carry there on שבת.

phrases.english: because the salt holds up the beam
and the beam holds the salt in place,
even isterokanit salt works,
and they do not disagree:
this ruling is where there is a beam,
that ruling is where there is no beam.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a different way, other than רב פפא's, to show that רב and שמואל do not really disagree.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Splitting the two rulings into two different cases (with a beam and without a beam)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: רב and שמואל seem to argue directly about whether salt can serve as a מחיצה.
steps.terutzMaskana: שמואל allows salt when a beam presses it down. רב forbids salt with no beam.

steps.title: Why must a mill be kept away from the wall?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the משנה's rule about keeping a mill away from a neighbor's wall and asks for the reason.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה said: We keep a mill three handbreadths from the lower stone, which is four from the upper stone, and so on. What is the reason?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves to a new line of the משנה about mills. It asks why the distance is needed, and the answer comes in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה gives a measurement but no reason. The גמרא wants to know what kind of harm the distance prevents, because that tells us what the rule is really about.

keyTerms.meaning: The lower millstone, which stays still
The upper millstone, which turns (literally, the rider)

phrases.english: We distance the mill
three handbreadths from the lower stone,
which is four from the upper stone, etc.
phrases.notes: The upper stone is narrower, so three from the bottom stone comes out to four from the top stone.

phrases.english: What is the reason?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new topic from the משנה, unrelated to the salt discussion.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What harm does keeping the mill away from the wall prevent?

steps.title: First answer: because of shaking
steps.stepSummary: The reason is the shaking the mill causes, which could damage the neighbor's wall.
steps.simpleTranslation: Because of the shaking.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a first answer: the mill shakes the ground, and that can harm the wall next door.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If shaking is the reason, the rule protects the wall from being physically damaged. The next step will test whether this reason fits every case.

phrases.english: Because of the shaking.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 15.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The distance is needed because the mill's shaking could damage the wall.

steps.title: A ברייתא about a mill on a wooden stand, where there is no shaking
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא requires the same distance even for a mill set on a wooden stand (a 'חמור'), which does not touch the ground and so causes no shaking. So shaking cannot be the reason.
steps.simpleTranslation: But a ברייתא teaches: And a mill on a 'חמור' stand must be three handbreadths from the lower stone, which is four from the opening where the grain goes in. There, what shaking is there?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the answer of step 16. It brings a ברייתא that requires a distance even for a mill that does not shake.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the only reason were shaking, a mill that does not shake would not need any distance. Since the ברייתא still requires one, there must be a different reason.

keyTerms.meaning: But a ברייתא teaches (introduces a challenge from a ברייתא)
A mill set on a wooden stand called a 'חמור', so it does not touch the ground
The opening at the top where the grain is poured in

phrases.english: But isn't it taught in a baraita:
And one set on a 'donkey' stand
phrases.notes: The 'חמור' here is a wooden stand the mill sits on, so the mill doesn't touch the ground and can't shake it.

phrases.english: must be three handbreadths from the base stone,
which is four from the opening for the grain.
There, what shaking is there?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the reason given in step 16.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that the distance is needed because of shaking.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A mill raised on a wooden stand does not shake the ground, yet it still needs a distance, so shaking cannot be the reason.

steps.title: The real reason: because of the noise
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא drops the shaking reason and says the distance is needed because of the mill's noise.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, it is because of the noise.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives up its first answer and replaces it with a new reason that also fits the mill on a stand: noise.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Every mill makes noise, including one raised on a stand that does not shake the ground. So noise explains both the משנה and the ברייתא, which shaking could not do.

keyTerms.meaning: Rather (drops the earlier answer and gives a new one)

steps.whatToRemember: A mill is kept away from the neighbor's wall because of its noise, not its shaking.
steps.confusionAlert: Don't keep the first answer (shaking) as the conclusion. The word אלא tells you the גמרא threw it out.

phrases.english: Rather, it is because of the noise.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 17 by replacing the reason.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Replacing the earlier reason with a new one
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The distance is needed because of shaking.
steps.terutzMaskana: The distance is needed because of noise, which is true of every mill.

steps.title: אביי: an oven's base is one handbreadth wider than its rim
steps.stepSummary: From the משנה's oven measurements (three from the base, four from the rim), אביי learns that an oven's base is one handbreadth wider than its rim. This matters when buying and selling ovens.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה said: And the oven must be three handbreadths from the base, which is four from the rim. אביי said: Learn from this that the base of an oven sticks out one handbreadth. This matters for buying and selling.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes the משנה's line about ovens, and אביי draws a fact about how ovens are built from the numbers.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Three handbreadths from the base equals four from the rim, so the base must stick out one handbreadth more than the rim. אביי says this matters in business: a buyer knows what a normal oven should look like.

keyTerms.meaning: The wide bottom of the oven
The rim or top edge of the oven

phrases.english: And the oven
must be three handbreadths from the base,
which is four from the rim.
Abaye said:
Learn from this that the base of an oven is a handbreadth
phrases.notes: He means the base sticks out one handbreadth past the rim.

phrases.english: The practical difference is for buying and selling.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves on to the next line of the משנה, about ovens.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: An oven's base is one handbreadth wider than its rim. This is the normal size when ovens are bought and sold.

steps.title: New משנה: an oven in a house needs four אמות of space above it
steps.stepSummary: A new משנה rules that an oven may not be set up inside a house unless there are four אמות of open space above it.
steps.simpleTranslation: משנה: A person may not set up an oven inside a house unless there is a height of four אמות above it.
steps.whatsHappening: A new משנה begins. It sets a safety rule: there must be four אמות of space between an oven and the ceiling.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ceiling is the floor of the home upstairs. Space above the oven keeps its heat from burning that ceiling and harming the neighbor above.

phrases.english: MISHNA:

phrases.aramaic: לֹא יַעֲמִיד אָדָם תַּנּוּר בְּתוֹךְ הַבַּיִת
phrases.english: A person may not set up an oven inside a house

phrases.aramaic: אֶלָּא אִם כֵּן יֵשׁ עַל גַּבָּיו
phrases.english: unless there is above it
a height of four cubits.

steps.triggerLanguage: לֹא יַעֲמִיד אָדָם תַּנּוּר בְּתוֹךְ הַבַּיִת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new משנה about ovens inside a house.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: An oven inside a house needs four אמות of space between it and the ceiling.

steps.title: An oven in an upper story needs a thick plaster floor beneath it
steps.stepSummary: An oven set up in an upper story needs a plaster floor three handbreadths thick beneath it. A stove needs only one handbreadth.
steps.simpleTranslation: If he was setting it up in an upper story, there must be a plaster floor three handbreadths thick beneath it. And for a stove, one handbreadth.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה continues with an oven placed upstairs. Now the worry is the ceiling below, so it needs a thick layer of plaster under it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Here the danger is downward: the oven could burn the ceiling of the home below. A כירה gives off less heat than a תנור, so a thinner layer of one handbreadth is enough.

keyTerms.meaning: A plaster floor laid over the ceiling beams
A stove, which is smaller than an oven

steps.whatToRemember: An oven inside a house needs four אמות of space above it. An oven upstairs needs three handbreadths of plaster below it, and a stove needs one.

phrases.english: If he was setting it up in an upper story,
there must be beneath it
a plaster floor three handbreadths thick.
And for a stove, one handbreadth.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the משנה, moving from an oven downstairs to an oven upstairs.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: An oven upstairs needs a plaster floor three handbreadths thick beneath it, and a stove needs one handbreadth.

steps.title: Even after keeping the distance, he pays for damage
steps.stepSummary: The משנה adds that if damage happens anyway, the owner of the oven or stove must pay.
steps.simpleTranslation: And if he causes damage, he pays for what he damaged.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה finishes its list of required distances. It says that keeping the distance does not free you from paying if damage still happens.
steps.deeperAnalysis: According to this view, the distances are only the minimum you must keep in order to be allowed to set things up. They do not protect you from paying. If damage happens, you are still responsible.

phrases.english: And if he caused damage –
phrases.notes: This means even after he kept all the distances listed in the משנה.

phrases.english: he pays for what he damaged.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes the משנה's distance rules by stating whether the owner is liable for damage.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Keeping the required distances does not free you from paying for damage that happens anyway.

steps.title: רבי שמעון: the distances free you from paying
steps.stepSummary: רבי שמעון says the whole point of the distances is that once you keep them, you are not liable.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי שמעון says: They only gave all these measurements to teach that if he keeps them and damage happens, he does not have to pay.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי שמעון disagrees with the previous line. He holds that keeping the measurements frees you from paying.
steps.deeperAnalysis: For רבי שמעון, the distances are the standard of proper care. If you kept them, you did everything required, so you are פטור. The first opinion sees the distances only as a minimum that still leaves you liable.
steps.confusionAlert: Do not mix up the two opinions. The first says that even after keeping the distance you still pay. רבי שמעון says that because you kept the distance, you do not pay.
steps.whyThisMatters: This sets up a basic disagreement in the laws of neighbors' damage: is a required distance only a minimum, or is it a full protection from liability?

phrases.english: Rabbi Shimon says:
They did not state all these measurements,
except so that if he caused damage –
he is exempt from paying.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן אוֹמֵר: לֹא אָמְרוּ כׇּל הַשִּׁיעוּרִין הָאֵלּוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Disagrees with the opinion in Step 22 about liability.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Once the measurements are kept, the owner is not liable for any damage that results.

steps.title: No bakery, dye shop or barn under a neighbor's storeroom
steps.stepSummary: A new משנה forbids setting up a bakery, a dye shop or a cattle barn underneath someone else's storeroom.
steps.simpleTranslation: A person may not open a bakery or a dye shop under his neighbor's storeroom, and he may not set up a cattle barn there either.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה starts a new case. You may not put a business underneath a neighbor's storeroom if it sends up damage.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Bakeries and dye shops give off heat and smoke, and a barn gives off smells. All of these rise and can ruin what is stored above. So the person below is not allowed to set them up.

phrases.english: A person may not open a shop
of bakers or of dyers
beneath his neighbor's storeroom,
and not a cattle barn.

steps.triggerLanguage: לֹא יִפְתַּח אָדָם חֲנוּת שֶׁל נַחְתּוֹמִין
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new משנה about damage that rises from below to a storeroom.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A bakery, dye shop or cattle barn may not be placed under a neighbor's storeroom.

steps.title: Wine storeroom: bakery allowed, barn not
steps.stepSummary: The משנה says that under a wine storeroom a bakery or dye shop is allowed, but a cattle barn is still forbidden.
steps.simpleTranslation: In truth, for a wine storeroom they permitted it, but not a cattle barn.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה makes an exception to the rule it just gave. It applies to a storeroom that holds wine.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Heat from a bakery or dye shop does not harm wine, so those are allowed under it. A barn's smell does harm wine, so the barn stays forbidden.

phrases.english: In truth, regarding wine they permitted,
phrases.notes: He means a storeroom of wine. Setting up a bakery or dye shop under it is allowed.

phrases.english: but not a cattle barn.

steps.whatToRemember: Under a neighbor's storeroom you may not put a bakery, a dye shop or a barn. If the storeroom holds wine, a bakery or dye shop is allowed, but a barn never is.
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Narrows the rule in Step 24 for a wine storeroom.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Under a wine storeroom a bakery or dye shop is permitted, but a cattle barn is not.

steps.title: A ברייתא gives thicker plaster measurements
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the משנה from Step 21 with a ברייתא that requires four handbreadths of plaster for an oven and three for a stove.
steps.simpleTranslation: But it was taught in a ברייתא: for an oven, four handbreadths, and for a stove, three!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא goes back to the earlier משנה, which required three handbreadths of plaster under an oven and one under a stove. It points out that a ברייתא gives larger numbers.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה says three for an oven and one for a stove. The ברייתא says four for an oven and three for a stove. The two sources seem to contradict each other.

phrases.english: GEMARA: But it was taught:
For an oven, four,
phrases.notes: Four handbreadths of plaster underneath, compared with three in the משנה (Step 21).

phrases.english: and for a stove, three!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Returns to the plaster measurements of Step 21 and challenges them.
steps.kashyaTarget: The משנה's measurements of three handbreadths for an oven and one for a stove.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A ברייתא requires larger amounts (four and three), so the two sources contradict each other.

steps.title: אביי: the ברייתא is about bakers' ovens
steps.stepSummary: אביי explains that the ברייתא is talking about bakers' ovens and stoves, which get much hotter.
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי said: That ברייתא is about bakers. Our ordinary oven is like a baker's stove.
steps.whatsHappening: אביי answers the contradiction by saying the two sources describe different kinds of ovens.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Bakers use their ovens all day, so they get much hotter and need thicker plaster. An ordinary home oven is only as hot as a baker's stove, which is why both require three handbreadths. The משנה and the ברייתא are dealing with different cases, so they do not disagree.

keyTerms.meaning: ours (the ordinary one in our משנה)

phrases.english: Abaye said:
When that was taught – it was about those of bakers,
for our oven
is like a stove of bakers.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר אַבָּיֵי: כִּי תַּנְיָא הָהִיא בִּדְנַחְתּוֹמִין
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the קשיא of Step 26.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Splitting the cases (the two sources describe different situations)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: We might have thought the ברייתא and the משנה describe the same ovens and contradict each other.
steps.terutzMaskana: The ברייתא describes bakers' ovens, which are hotter. An ordinary oven matches a baker's stove, so both need three handbreadths.

steps.title: A barn that came first may stay
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא teaches that if the cattle barn was there before the storeroom, it is allowed to remain.
steps.simpleTranslation: On the משנה 'One may not open a shop': A ברייתא taught that if the barn was there before the storeroom, it is permitted.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא turns to the second משנה. It brings a ברייתא that limits the rule against a barn.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ban applies only when someone sets up a barn under a storeroom that already exists. If the barn was there first, the storeroom owner cannot force it to move.

phrases.english: "One may not open a shop," etc.
It was taught: If the barn was
earlier than the storeroom – it is permitted.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּנָא: אִם הָיְתָה רֶפֶת קוֹדֶמֶת לָאוֹצָר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves on to the משנה of Step 24 and adds a limit to it.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A barn that was there before the storeroom may stay where it is.

steps.title: Does a prepared but empty storeroom count?
steps.stepSummary: אביי asks what the law is if the room was cleaned and sprinkled as a storeroom but not yet filled.
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי asked: If he swept and sprinkled the room to use it as a storeroom, what is the law?
steps.whatsHappening: אביי asks a question based on the ברייתא. Does a room that has only been prepared already count as a storeroom that 'came first'?
steps.deeperAnalysis: If preparing the room is enough, a barn can no longer be set up beneath it. If the room must actually hold produce, a barn can still be placed below it while it is empty. The גמרא never decides this; step 30 ends the series with תיקו.

keyTerms.meaning: swept and sprinkled water (to keep down dust)

phrases.english: Abaye asked:
If he swept and sprinkled it for a storeroom,
what is the law?

steps.triggerLanguage: בָּעֵי אַבָּיֵי: כִּיבֵּד וְרִיבֵּץ לְאוֹצָר, מַהוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks how the 'who came first' rule of Step 28 applies to a room that was only prepared.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Does preparing a room as a storeroom make it count as an existing storeroom, so that no barn may then be set up beneath it?

steps.title: More signs of a storeroom: windows, a veranda, an upper room
steps.stepSummary: אביי continues asking which actions make a room count as a storeroom: adding windows, building a veranda beneath it, or building an upper room. None of these questions is answered.
steps.simpleTranslation: If he added windows, what is the law? If there is an enclosed veranda under the storeroom, what is the law? If he built an upper room on top of his house, what is the law? The question stays unresolved.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא continues אביי's list of questions from Step 29 with three more cases. Each one asks whether this preparation is already enough to make the room count as a storeroom.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The real question is when a room becomes an 'אוצר'. That matters because a barn that was there first may stay (Step 28). Each case is a different kind of preparation for storage, but none of them actually fills the room. No source decides any of them, so the גמרא says תיקו.

keyTerms.meaning: a veranda or covered porch area
'let it stand': the question stays unresolved

phrases.english: If he added windows, what is the law?
phrases.notes: Windows let air in, which is how you prepare a room to store produce.

phrases.english: An enclosed veranda beneath the storeroom, what is the law?

phrases.aramaic: בָּנָה עֲלִיָּיה עַל גַּבֵּי בֵּיתוֹ, מַהוּ?
phrases.english: If he built an upper room on top of his house, what is the law?
It stands unresolved.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues אביי's series of questions from Step 29.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Does adding windows, a veranda, or an upper room make a space count as a storeroom, so that a newer barn underneath it is forbidden?
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: No answer is given; the question is left as תיקו.

steps.title: רב הונא asks about dates and pomegranates
steps.stepSummary: רב הונא בריה דרב יהושע asks whether putting dates and pomegranates in the room makes it a storeroom. This question is also left unresolved.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב הונא, son of רב יהושע, asked: dates and pomegranates, what is the law? It stays unresolved.
steps.whatsHappening: Another אמורא adds a similar question: does storing dates and pomegranates in the room count as starting to use it as a storeroom? Again, there is no answer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Unlike the earlier questions, here something is actually put into the room. The question is whether placing dates and pomegranates there already counts as starting to use it as a storeroom. No answer is found, so the question stays תיקו.

keyTerms.meaning: he asked (a real question looking for an answer)

steps.whatToRemember: All the questions about when a room becomes a storeroom stay unresolved (תיקו).

phrases.aramaic: בָּעֵי רַב הוּנָא בְּרֵיהּ דְּרַב יְהוֹשֻׁעַ:
phrases.english: Rav Huna, son of Rav Yehoshua, asked:
Dates and pomegranates, what is the law?
phrases.notes: He means: if he put these into the room, does it now count as a storeroom?

phrases.english: It stands unresolved.

steps.triggerLanguage: בָּעֵי רַב הוּנָא בְּרֵיהּ דְּרַב יְהוֹשֻׁעַ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a parallel question from a different אמורא, which closes the series.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Does storing dates and pomegranates make the room a storeroom?

steps.title: Why wine is allowed but a cattle barn is not
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the משנה's line about wine and brings a ברייתא with the reason: heat and smoke improve wine, but a cattle barn makes it smell bad.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'In truth they permitted with wine, etc.' A ברייתא taught: they permitted it with wine because it improves the wine, and not a cattle barn because it makes the wine smell.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא goes back to the משנה from Step 25 and gives the reason behind its ruling.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Normally a bakery under a storeroom is a problem because the heat ruins produce. Wine is different, because the heat and smoke actually improve it. A cattle barn is still forbidden, since its smell spoils the wine.

keyTerms.meaning: 'in truth': the phrase that introduces the משנה's ruling

phrases.english: 'In truth, they permitted with wine, etc.'
It was taught: They permitted with wine
because it improves it,
phrases.notes: The heat and smoke from the oven help the wine.

phrases.english: but not a cattle barn,
because it makes it smell bad.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Goes back to the משנה in Step 25 to explain its reason.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A bakery or dye shop may be under a wine storeroom because the heat improves wine; a cattle barn may not, because its smell spoils it.

steps.title: רב יוסף: our wine is too delicate
steps.stepSummary: רב יוסף says that the wine in his place is so sensitive that even a candle's smoke harms it.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יוסף said: this wine of ours, even the smoke of a candle harms it.
steps.whatsHappening: רב יוסף adds a practical limit to the ברייתא's reason for his own local wine.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא assumed that smoke improves wine. רב יוסף points out that this depends on the type of wine. His local wine is so delicate that even a tiny amount of smoke damages it, so the leniency would not apply to it.

phrases.english: Rav Yosef said: This (wine) of ours,

phrases.aramaic: אֲפִילּוּ קוּטְרָא דִּשְׁרָגָא נָמֵי קַשְׁיָא לֵיהּ.
phrases.english: even the smoke of a candle also harms it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Limits the ברייתא's reason so it does not cover delicate wine.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: For רב יוסף's local wine, even candle smoke is harmful, so the 'smoke improves wine' reason does not apply to it.

steps.title: רב ששת: alfalfa is like a cattle barn
steps.stepSummary: רב ששת rules that storing alfalfa under a wine storeroom is treated like a cattle barn and is forbidden.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב ששת said: alfalfa is like a cattle barn.
steps.whatsHappening: רב ששת adds another item that falls into the forbidden category of the cattle barn.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A cattle barn is forbidden because of its smell (Step 32). Alfalfa rots and also gives off a bad smell, so it has the same effect on the wine and gets the same rule.

phrases.english: Rav Sheshet said:
And alfalfa is like a cattle barn.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב שֵׁשֶׁת: וְאַסְפַּסְתָּא כְּרֶפֶת בָּקָר דָּמְיָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Extends the cattle-barn rule to another item that smells.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Alfalfa may not be placed under a wine storeroom, just like a cattle barn.
steps.whatToRemember: Heat and smoke are fine for wine (except very delicate wine), but anything that smells, like a barn or alfalfa, is forbidden under a wine storeroom.

steps.title: New משנה: a store in the courtyard versus noisy work at home
steps.stepSummary: A neighbor can stop someone from opening a store in their shared courtyard because the customers' noise keeps him awake. He cannot stop a craftsman who makes utensils at home and sells them in the market, even if the hammer, mill, or children are noisy.
steps.simpleTranslation: A store in a courtyard: the neighbor can protest and say, 'I can't sleep because of the noise of people coming in and going out.' But one who makes utensils goes out and sells them in the market, and the neighbor cannot protest and say, 'I can't sleep,' not because of the hammer, not because of the mill, and not because of the children.
steps.whatsHappening: A new משנה begins about noise between neighbors who share a courtyard. It gives two cases with opposite outcomes.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the first case, the neighbor may block a store because of the noise from customers coming and going. In the second case, he may not block noisy work like hammering or grinding, or the noise of children, as long as the selling happens in the market. That looks surprising, since both cases involve noise, and the גמרא will ask about it next.

phrases.english: MISHNA: A store in a courtyard:
he can protest against him and say to him:
phrases.notes: 'He' is a neighbor who shares the courtyard.

phrases.english: I cannot sleep
because of the noise of those coming in and those going out.
But one may make utensils
and go out and sell them in the market,

phrases.aramaic: וְאֵינוֹ יָכוֹל לִמְחוֹת בְּיָדוֹ וְלוֹמַר לוֹ:
phrases.english: and he cannot protest against him and say to him:
I cannot sleep
not because of the noise of the hammer,
and not because of the noise of the mill,
and not because of the noise of the children.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new topic: noise disturbances in a shared courtyard.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A neighbor can block a store in the shared courtyard, but cannot block noisy home crafts, mill work, or children's noise when the goods are sold in the market.
steps.whyThisMatters: This is a basic source for which kinds of noise neighbors must accept and which they can prevent.

steps.title: Why is the first case different from the second?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why the noise of customers is grounds to protest while the noise of a hammer or mill is not.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is different about the first clause, and what is different about the last clause?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא points out that the two halves of the משנה seem to contradict each other.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Both halves deal with noise that disturbs a neighbor's sleep. Yet the first half lets the neighbor protest and the second half does not. The גמרא wants the reason for this difference.
steps.confusionAlert: A hammer is probably louder than customers, which is exactly why the גמרא is bothered. Don't assume the second case is allowed because it is quieter.

phrases.english: GEMARA: What is different about the first clause,
and what is different about the last clause?

steps.triggerLanguage: מַאי שְׁנָא רֵישָׁא, וּמַאי שְׁנָא סֵיפָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the inner logic of the משנה just quoted.
steps.kashyaTarget: The two clauses of the משנה in Step 35.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Both clauses involve noise that stops a neighbor from sleeping, so why can he protest in one but not the other?

steps.title: אביי: the second case is in a different courtyard
steps.stepSummary: אביי answers that the last clause is about noise coming from a different courtyard, which a neighbor cannot block.
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי said: in the last clause, we have come to a different courtyard.
steps.whatsHappening: אביי resolves the contradiction by saying the two clauses are about different places.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the first clause the store is in the protester's own shared courtyard, so he can object. In the last clause the noisy work is in another courtyard, so he has no right to object. The difference is location, not the type of noise.

keyTerms.meaning: we have come to (a different case)

phrases.english: Abaye said:
In the last clause we have come to a different courtyard.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the contradiction raised in Step 36.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Divides the clauses into two different settings (same courtyard vs. another courtyard).
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Both clauses are about the same shared courtyard, so they contradict each other.
steps.terutzMaskana: The last clause is about a different courtyard, where the neighbor has no right to protest.

steps.title: רבא rejects אביי and starts his own answer
steps.stepSummary: רבא objects that if the משנה meant a different courtyard, it should have said so clearly. He then begins his own answer.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said to him: if so, let it teach, 'In a different courtyard it is permitted!' Rather, רבא said:
steps.whatsHappening: רבא challenges אביי's answer from the wording of the משנה. He then starts to give his own explanation, which continues on the next amud.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the whole difference were that the noise comes from a different courtyard, the משנה should have said so openly: 'in a different courtyard it is permitted.' Since it does not say this, רבא rejects אביי's reading and gives his own answer.

keyTerms.meaning: let it teach / it should have said

phrases.english: Rava said to him:
If so, let it teach:
'In a different courtyard it is permitted!'
Rather, Rava said:

steps.triggerLanguage: אִי הָכִי, לִיתְנֵי: חָצֵר אַחֶרֶת מוּתָּר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects אביי's answer in Step 37 and introduces רבא's alternative.
steps.kashyaTarget: אביי's claim that the last clause is about a different courtyard.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If that were the case, the משנה should simply have said 'a different courtyard is permitted' instead of describing the work in detail.
